s: sword of the Princes has point the Wise and brave
q: The Wise and brave," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "are its point.

s: sword of the Princes has edge the incorruptible
q: The incorruptible are its edge.

s: sword of the Princes has back the virtuous
q: The virtuous are its back.

s: sword of the Princes has hilt the loyal
q: The loyal are its hilt.

s: sword of the Princes has sheath the heroic
q: The heroic are its sheath.

s: sword of the People has dishevelled hair (hanging over its temples)
q: The sword of the People," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "has dishevelled hair hanging over its temples.

s: sword of the People wears slouching cap (with coarse tangled tassel)
q: It wears a slouching cap with coarse tangled tassel

s: sword of the People wears short-tailed coat
q: and a short-tailed coat.

s: Wên Wang of Chao holds bouts (day and night)
q: Day and night they had bouts before the prince.

s: sword of the People is like game-cock
q: It is like a game-cock.

s: the people constitute sword of the People (symbolically)
q: The sword of the People," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "has dishevelled hair hanging over its temples.

s: Chuang Tzŭ criticizes Wên Wang of Chao (for devoting himself to the sword of the People)
q: Now you, great prince, wield sovereign power, and yet you devote yourself to this sword of the People. I am truly ashamed of it.

s: new order of things is accepted by swordsmen (submissively)
q: After this the prince did not quit his palace for three months, while the swordsmen, submitting to the new order of things, died in their own homes.

s: Wên Wang of Chao is satisfied with sword-play (never)
q: Yet the prince was never satisfied.

s: Wên Wang of Chao wields sovereign power
q: Now you, great prince, wield sovereign power, and yet you devote yourself to this sword of the People.

s: swordsmen are present in State of Chao (in large numbers)
q: Swordsmen thronged his halls, to the number of three thousand and more.

s: swordsmen have bouts (before Wên Wang of Chao, day and night)
q: Day and night they had bouts before the prince.

s: swordsmen are killed or wounded (about a hundred per year)
q: In the course of a year, a hundred or so would be killed or wounded.

s: Confucius is a Sage of Lu
q: "He is the Sage of Lu," replied Tzŭ Lu.

s: Confucius is steeped in deceit (early)
q: Alas! you, Sir, were early steeped in deceit, and are late in hearing the great doctrine.

s: Confucius respects the old fisherman (because he possesses TAO)
q: And as this old fisherman may be said to possess TAO, could I venture not to respect him?

s: the old fisherman is a fisherman (old)
q: Thereupon he followed the old man down the shore, catching him up just as he was drawing in his boat with his staff.

s: the old fisherman is a Sage
q: Tzŭ Kung went back and told Confucius, who, laying aside his lute, arose and said, "This man is a Sage!"

s: the old fisherman possesses TAO (may be said to)
q: And as this old fisherman may be said to possess TAO, could I venture not to respect him?

s: Tzŭ Lu serves Confucius (for a long time)
q: Master, I have been in your service now for a long time, yet never did I see you treat any man like this.

s: Yen Yüan brings up the chariot
q: Yen Yüan then brought up the chariot, and Tzŭ Lu offered the hand-cord to Confucius.

s: Confucius belongs to the K'ung family (by clan)
q: "Of what clan?" asked the old man. "Of the K'ung family," replied Tzŭ Lu.

s: the Son of Heaven is one of these four (proper functions)
q: The Son of Heaven, the princes, the ministers, and the people,--if these four fulfil their proper functions, the result is good government.

s: the Son of Heaven suffers from the sorrows of the Son of Heaven
q: The two great principles of nature working inharmoniously, heat and cold coming at irregular seasons so that men and things suffer, the princes rebellious and fighting among themselves so that the people perish, music and ceremonies ill regulated, wealth dissipated, the relationships of man disregarded, the masses sunk in immorality,--such are the sorrows which fall to the share of the Son of Heaven.

s: the people are a social class
q: The Son of Heaven, the princes, the ministers, and the people,--if these four fulfil their proper functions, the result is good government.

s: the people suffer from the sorrows of the people
q: Barren land, leaky roofs, want of food and clothing, inability to meet taxation, quarrels of wives and concubines, no precedence between young and old,--such are the sorrows of the people.

s: Confucius devotes himself to loyalty and truth
q: "He devotes himself," replied Tzŭ Lu, "to loyalty and truth.

s: the Black Forest contains Apricot Altar
q: Confucius, travelling in the Black Forest, rested awhile at Apricot Altar.

s: Apricot Altar is in the Black Forest
q: Confucius, travelling in the Black Forest, rested awhile at Apricot Altar.

s: the Ch'êns surround Confucius
q: I was surrounded by the Ch'êns and the Ts'ais.

s: the Ts'ais surround Confucius
q: I was surrounded by the Ch'êns and the Ts'ais.

s: the old fisherman's boat belongs to the old fisherman
q: Thereupon he followed the old man down the shore, catching him up just as he was drawing in his boat with his staff.

s: Confucius practises charity (towards his neighbour)
q: He practises charity and duty towards his neighbour.

s: the lute is played by Confucius
q: His disciples sat down to their books, and he himself played upon the lute and sang.

s: the chariot is brought up by Yen Yüan
q: Yen Yüan then brought up the chariot, and Tzŭ Lu offered the hand-cord to Confucius.

s: the hand-cord is offered to Confucius (by Tzŭ Lu)
q: Yen Yüan then brought up the chariot, and Tzŭ Lu offered the hand-cord to Confucius.

s: TAO is a source of all creation
q: Further. TAO is the source of all creation.

s: TAO gives life to men (when they have it)
q: Men have it, and live.

s: TAO is lost by men (with death as the result)
q: They lose it, and die.

s: TAO causes success affairs (when affairs accord with it)
q: Affairs in antagonism thereto, fail; in accordance therewith, succeed.

s: TAO is possessed by the old fisherman (as may be said)
q: And as this old fisherman may be said to possess TAO, could I venture not to respect him?

s: original purity is a perfection of truth unalloyed
q: Our original purity," replied the fisherman, "is the perfection of truth unalloyed.

s: Confucius practises duty to one's neighbour
q: He practises charity and duty towards his neighbour.

s: original purity is given by God
q: Our original purity is given to us from God.

s: original purity cannot be changed unchangeable
q: It is as it is, and cannot be changed.

s: original purity influences others (as a necessary basis)
q: Without this, we cannot influence others.

s: original purity underlies emotions (human emotions depend upon it)
q: Our emotions are dependent upon the original purity within; and accordingly we hold the latter in esteem.

s: charity is practised by Confucius (towards one's neighbour)
q: Now you occupy yourself with charity and duty to one's neighbour.

s: ceremonial regulated by you, Sir (to reform the masses)
q: But now you, Sir, occupying neither the more exalted position of ruler nor performing the subordinate functions of minister, nevertheless take upon yourself to regulate music and ceremonies and to distinguish the relationships of man, in order to reform the masses.

s: ceremonial are ill regulated ill regulated (a sorrow falling to the share of the Son of Heaven)
q: music and ceremonies ill regulated, wealth dissipated, the relationships of man disregarded, the masses sunk in immorality,--such are the sorrows which fall to the share of the Son of Heaven.

s: Confucius regulates ceremonial
q: He regulates ceremonies and music.

s: the four persecutions are suffered by Confucius
q: I know not what my fault is that I should have suffered these four persecutions.

s: Confucius distinguishes the relationships of man
q: He distinguishes the relationships of man.

s: Confucius is a student (from youth until his sixty-ninth year)
q: Yes, I have been a student from my youth upwards until now, the sixty-ninth year of my age.

s: Confucius has suffered the four persecutions
q: Twice was I driven from Lu. I was tabooed in Wei. My tree was cut down in Sung. I was surrounded by the Ch'êns and the Ts'ais. I know not what my fault is that I should have suffered these four persecutions.

s: Lieh Tzŭ is a allegorical personage (possibly created by Chuang Tzŭ)
q: His record is not given by the historian Ssŭ-ma Ch'ien, and he may well have been no more than an allegorical personage created by Chuang Tzŭ for purposes of illustration.

s: Chuang Tzŭ knows TAO (with speech regarded as artificial)
q: Chuang Tzŭ said, "To know TAO is easy. The difficulty lies in the elimination of speech.

s: Chuang Tzŭ declines service to prince (comparing office to becoming a sacrificial ox)
q: Some prince having invited Chuang Tzŭ to enter his service, Chuang Tzŭ said in reply to the envoy, "Sir, have you ever noticed a sacrificial ox?

s: Chuang Tzŭ has disciples disciples (at the time of his death)
q: When Chuang Tzŭ was about to die, his disciples expressed a wish to give him a splendid funeral.

s: Confucius is a man of outward show (according to Yen Ho)
q: Confucius is a man of outward show and of specious words.

s: Confucius is considered dangerous to Lu (if made a pillar of the realm)
q: "Were I to make Confucius a pillar of my realm, would the State be profited thereby?" "It would be most perilous!" replied Yen Ho.

s: Confucius has tests of superior man (loyalty, respectfulness, ability, knowledge, trustworthiness, integrity, fidelity, decorum, and morality)
q: Thus the loyalty of the superior man is tested by employing him at a distance, his respectfulness by employing him near at hand. His ability, by troublesome missions. His knowledge, by unexpected questions. His trustworthiness, by specification of time limits. His integrity by entrusting him with money. His fidelity, by dangerous tasks. His decorum, by filling him with wine. His morality, by placing him in disreputable surroundings.

s: TAO is known by Nature (without speech)
q: To know TAO without speech appertains to the natural.

s: Sage regards certainties as uncertainties (therefore never up in arms)
q: The true Sage regards certainties as uncertainties; therefore he is never up in arms.

s: Lieh Tzŭ is associated with TAO (name well known in connection with it)
q: Lieh Yü K'ou, a name well known in connection with TAO.

s: Duke Ai of Lu asked Yen Ho
q: Duke Ai of Lu asked Yen Ho, saying, "Were I to make Confucius a pillar of my realm, would the State be profited thereby?"

s: Yen Ho opposes Confucius (as a pillar of the realm)
q: "It would be most perilous!" replied Yen Ho. "Confucius is a man of outward show and of specious words.

s: Hsü Yu is compared with which of them (of old)
q: Which of them can be compared with Hsü Yu of old?

s: Heaven is a coffin and shell (for Chuang Tzŭ's funeral)
q: With Heaven and Earth for my coffin and shell; with the sun, moon, and stars as my burial regalia; and with all creation to escort me to the grave,--are not my funeral paraphernalia ready to hand?

s: Earth is a coffin and shell (for Chuang Tzŭ's funeral)
q: With Heaven and Earth for my coffin and shell; with the sun, moon, and stars as my burial regalia; and with all creation to escort me to the grave,--are not my funeral paraphernalia ready to hand?

s: TAO is inscrutable mystery (not penetrated by ordinary intelligence)
q: Yet he would penetrate the mystery of TAO and of creation, and rise to participation in the ONE.

s: THE UNIVERSE escorts Chuang Tzŭ (to the grave)
q: With Heaven and Earth for my coffin and shell; with the sun, moon, and stars as my burial regalia; and with all creation to escort me to the grave,--are not my funeral paraphernalia ready to hand?

s: funeral desired by Chuang Tzŭ (a splendid funeral)
q: When Chuang Tzŭ was about to die, his disciples expressed a wish to give him a splendid funeral.

s: Poh Hun Wu Jen warns against external influence (as a danger to natural constitution)
q: Exerting influence thus unduly over others, you are by them influenced in turn. You disturb your natural constitution, and are of no further account.

s: Virtue is unconscious possession (in men of true virtue)
q: Wherefore it follows that men of true virtue are unconscious of its possession.

s: Virtue is damaged by intentional practice (when the mind looks outwards)
q: There is nothing more fatal than intentional virtue, when the mind looks outwards.

s: Virtue has sources of injury five (eyes, nose, mouth, ears, and thought)
q: There are five sources of injury to virtue. Eyes, nose, mouth, ears, and thought.

s: TAO informs the Canon of Rites (with adaptability)
q: It informs the Canon of _Poetry_ with its vigour, the Canon of _History_ with its usefulness, the Canon of _Rites_ with its adaptability, the Canon of _Music_ with its harmonising influence, the Canon of _Changes_ with its mysterious Principles, and the _Spring and Autumn_ with its discriminations.

s: TAO informs the Canon of Music (with harmonising influence)
q: It informs the Canon of _Poetry_ with its vigour, the Canon of _History_ with its usefulness, the Canon of _Rites_ with its adaptability, the Canon of _Music_ with its harmonising influence, the Canon of _Changes_ with its mysterious Principles, and the _Spring and Autumn_ with its discriminations.

s: TAO is scattered in the world (in fragments when the world is disorganised)
q: For the system of TAO is scattered in fragments over the face of the earth.

s: Sage is a ideal man (one of four denominations)
q: These are but four different denominations of the ideal man.

s: Sage does not separate from the Source (as a condition of unity with God)
q: He who does not separate from the Source is one with God.

s: Sage is one with God (by not separating from the Source)
q: He who does not separate from the Source is one with God.

s: TAO exists everywhere nowhere (without exception)
q: There is nowhere where it does not come in.

s: Chou has scholars scholars (who clarified TAO in the Canons)
q: Its presence in the Canons of _Poetry_, _History_, _Rites_, and _Music_, has been made clear by many scholars of Chou and Lu.

s: Lu has scholars scholars (who clarified TAO in the Canons)
q: Its presence in the Canons of _Poetry_, _History_, _Rites_, and _Music_, has been made clear by many scholars of Chou and Lu.

s: Mih Tzŭ is a enthusiastic follower of TAO (with Ch'in Hua Li)
q: Mih Tzŭ and Ch'in Hua Li A disciple of Mih Tzŭ. became enthusiastic followers of TAO, but they pushed the system too far, carrying their practice

s: Ch'in Hua Li is a enthusiastic follower of TAO (with Mih Tzŭ)
q: Mih Tzŭ and Ch'in Hua Li A disciple of Mih Tzŭ. became enthusiastic followers of TAO, but they pushed the system too far, carrying their practice

s: Mih Tzŭ wrote Against Music (an essay)
q: The former wrote an essay _Against Music_, and another which he entitled _Economy_.

s: Mih Tzŭ wrote Economy (an essay)
q: The former wrote an essay _Against Music_, and another which he entitled _Economy_.

s: Mih Tzŭ advocated the system of universal love and beneficence (without contentions or censure)
q: He taught universal love and beneficence towards one's fellow men, without contentions, without censure of others.

s: Mih Tzŭ rejected music (in life)
q: There was to be no singing in life, no mourning after death.

s: TAO has source God (in the true Sage's ideal)
q: He who makes God the source, and TÊ the root, and TAO the portal, passively falling in with the modifications of his environment,--he is the true Sage.

s: Mih Tzŭ rejected mourning (after death)
q: There was to be no singing in life, no mourning after death.

s: Mih Tzŭ was well meaning well-meaning man (despite failure)
q: Nevertheless, Mih Tzŭ was undoubtedly a well-meaning man.

s: Mih Tzŭ is a man of genius (despite failure)
q: He may be called a man of genius.

s: Mihists practise self-mortification (as their end and aim)
q: And because he thus sacrificed himself to the commonwealth, ages of Mihists to come would also wear short serge jackets and straw sandals, and toil day and night without stopping, making self-mortification their end and aim

s: Mihists follow the TAO of Yü (by imitating Yü's toil)
q: If we cannot do this, we do not follow the TAO of Yü, and are unworthy to be called Mihists.

s: Sung Hsing is a enthusiastic follower of TAO (with Yin Wên)
q: Sung Hsing and Yin Wên became enthusiastic followers of TAO.

s: Yin Wên is a enthusiastic follower of TAO (with Sung Hsing)
q: Sung Hsing and Yin Wên became enthusiastic followers of TAO.

s: Sung Hsing wore a cap shaped like the Hua Mountain (as a badge)
q: They adopted a cap, shaped like the Hua Mountain, as a badge.

s: Yin Wên wore a cap shaped like the Hua Mountain (as a badge)
q: They adopted a cap, shaped like the Hua Mountain, as a badge.

s: Sung Hsing sought the tranquillity of the world (with a view to prolonging life)
q: Not to be involved in the mundane, not to indulge in the specious, not to be overreaching with the individual, nor antagonistic to the public; but to desire the tranquillity of the world in general with a view to the prolongation of life

s: TAO has root TÊ (in the true Sage's ideal)
q: He who makes God the source, and TÊ the root, and TAO the portal, passively falling in with the modifications of his environment,--he is the true Sage.

s: Yin Wên sought the tranquillity of the world (with a view to prolonging life)
q: Not to be involved in the mundane, not to indulge in the specious, not to be overreaching with the individual, nor antagonistic to the public; but to desire the tranquillity of the world in general with a view to the prolongation of life

s: the world rejected Sung Hsing (despite his efforts for peace)
q: Though the world would have none of them, yet they struggled on and would not give way.

s: the world rejected Yin Wên (despite his efforts for peace)
q: Though the world would have none of them, yet they struggled on and would not give way.

s: P'êng Mêng is a enthusiastic follower of TAO (with T'ien P'ien and Shên Tao)
q: P'êng Mêng, T'ien P'ien, and Shên Tao, became enthusiastic followers of TAO.

s: T'ien P'ien is a enthusiastic follower of TAO (with P'êng Mêng and Shên Tao)
q: P'êng Mêng, T'ien P'ien, and Shên Tao, became enthusiastic followers of TAO.

s: Shên Tao is a enthusiastic follower of TAO (with P'êng Mêng and T'ien P'ien)
q: P'êng Mêng, T'ien P'ien, and Shên Tao, became enthusiastic followers of TAO.

s: Shên Tao became a fatalist (after discarding all knowledge and self-interest)
q: Consequently, Shên Tao discarded all knowledge and self-interest and became a fatalist.

s: fatalism is associated with TAO (difficult to apprehend apart from it)
q: It is about as difficult to apprehend TAO apart from fatalism as the omniscience of God apart from predestination.

s: Kuan Yin is a enthusiastic follower of TAO (with Lao Tzŭ)
q: Kuan Yin and Lao Tzŭ became enthusiastic followers of TAO.

s: Lao Tzŭ is a enthusiastic follower of TAO (with Kuan Yin)
q: Kuan Yin and Lao Tzŭ became enthusiastic followers of TAO.

s: TAO nourishes all creation (as companion of the gods and purifier of the universe)
q: The companion of the gods, the purifier of the universe, it nourishes all creation, it unites the empire, it benefits the masses.

s: Kuan Yin based system on nothingness (with ONE as criterion)
q: They based their system upon nothingness, with ONE as their criterion.

s: Lao Tzŭ based system on nothingness (with ONE as criterion)
q: They based their system upon nothingness, with ONE as their criterion.

s: Kuan Yin used as criterion ONE (in a system based upon nothingness)
q: They based their system upon nothingness, with ONE as their criterion.

s: Lao Tzŭ used as criterion ONE (in a system based upon nothingness)
q: They based their system upon nothingness, with ONE as their criterion.

s: Kuan Yin advocated gentleness and humility (as outward expression)
q: Their outward expression was gentleness and humility.

s: Lao Tzŭ advocated gentleness and humility (as outward expression)
q: Their outward expression was gentleness and humility.

s: Lao Tzŭ valued weakness (as a strength-bearing condition)
q: He who conscious of being strong, is content to be weak,--he shall be a cynosure of men.

s: Lao Tzŭ valued the lowest place (when others strive to be first)
q: He who when others strive to be first, contents himself with the lowest place, is said to accept the contumely of the world.

s: Kuan Yin was Sage (as affirmed by the text)
q: O Kuan Yin! O Lao Tzŭ! verily ye were the true Sages of old.

s: Lao Tzŭ was Sage (as affirmed by the text)
q: O Kuan Yin! O Lao Tzŭ! verily ye were the true Sages of old.

s: TAO unites the Empire (as companion of the gods and purifier of the universe)
q: The companion of the gods, the purifier of the universe, it nourishes all creation, it unites the empire, it benefits the masses.

s: Chuang Tzŭ is a enthusiastic follower of TAO (as characterized in the text)
q: Chuang Tzŭ became an enthusiastic follower of TAO.

s: Chuang Tzŭ used goblet words (to speak in a corrupt age)
q: Therefore he employed "goblet words" which apply in various directions; he based his statements upon weighty authority in order to inspire confidence; and he put words in other people's mouths in order to secure breadth.

s: the book of Chuang Tzŭ is a extraordinary production (plausible and harmless enough)
q: Although his book is an extraordinary production, it is plausible and harmless enough.

s: Chuang Tzŭ roams with God (above)
q: Above, he roams with God.

s: Chuang Tzŭ consorts with the higher powers (in harmony between man and higher powers)
q: In relation to TAO, he establishes a harmony between man and the higher powers.

s: Chuang Tzŭ responds to environment (by yielding to modifications of existence)
q: Nevertheless, he yields to the modifications of existence and responds to the exigencies of environment.

s: the ancients practised self-discipline (while lenient to others' faults)
q: Not to covet posthumous fame, nor to aim at dazzling the world, nor to pose as a benefactor of mankind, but to be a strict self-disciplinarian while lenient to the faults of others,--herein lay the TAO of the ancients.

s: Yellow Emperor gave Hsien-ch'ih (a famous musical composition)
q: The Yellow Emperor gave us the _Hsien-ch'ih_.

s: Yao gave Ta-chang (a famous musical composition)
q: Yao gave us the _Ta-chang_.

s: TAO benefits the masses (as companion of the gods and purifier of the universe)
q: The companion of the gods, the purifier of the universe, it nourishes all creation, it unites the empire, it benefits the masses.

s: Great Yü drained the flood of waters (through the nine divisions and adjacent parts)
q: Of old, the great Yü drained off the flood of waters, and caused rivers and streams to flow through the nine divisions of the empire and the parts adjacent thereto

s: the flood of waters was drained by Great Yü (of old)
q: Of old, the great Yü drained off the flood of waters, and caused rivers and streams to flow through the nine divisions of the empire and the parts adjacent thereto

s: TAO informs the Canon of Poetry (with vigour)
q: It informs the Canon of _Poetry_ with its vigour, the Canon of _History_ with its usefulness, the Canon of _Rites_ with its adaptability, the Canon of _Music_ with its harmonising influence, the Canon of _Changes_ with its mysterious Principles, and the _Spring and Autumn_ with its discriminations.

s: TAO informs the Canon of History (with usefulness)
q: It informs the Canon of _Poetry_ with its vigour, the Canon of _History_ with its usefulness, the Canon of _Rites_ with its adaptability, the Canon of _Music_ with its harmonising influence, the Canon of _Changes_ with its mysterious Principles, and the _Spring and Autumn_ with its discriminations.

s: Hui Tzŭ is a philosopher (great and subtle)
q: Accordingly, Hui Tzŭ was regarded as a great philosopher and a very subtle dialectician; and became a favourite with the other dialecticians of the day.

s: Hui Tzŭ says The universe does not hold my peer.
q: and used to say, "The universe does not hold my peer."

s: Hui Tzŭ is devoid of sound system
q: Hui Tzŭ makes a parade of his strength, but is devoid of any sound system.

s: Hui Tzŭ is morally weak
q: Morally, he was weak; physically, he was violent.

s: Hui Tzŭ is physically violent
q: Morally, he was weak; physically, he was violent.

s: Hui Tzŭ has way dark and narrow way
q: His was a dark and narrow way.

s: Hui Tzŭ is a specialist specialist (possibly successful in that role)
q: As a specialist, he might have succeeded.

s: Hui Tzŭ has reputation as sophist
q: though he only succeeded in securing the reputation of a sophist.

s: Hui Tzŭ's doctrines are paradoxical
q: his doctrines are paradoxical, and his terms are used ambiguously.

s: Hui Tzŭ's doctrines use terms ambiguously
q: his doctrines are paradoxical, and his terms are used ambiguously.

s: Hui Tzŭ is a dialectician (very subtle)
q: Accordingly, Hui Tzŭ was regarded as a great philosopher and a very subtle dialectician; and became a favourite with the other dialecticians of the day.

s: heaven and earth are equally low equal low level (according to Hui Tzŭ)
q: That heaven and earth are equally low.

s: heaven and earth are impartial to universe (covering and supporting all)
q: That he loves all creation equally, just as heaven and earth are impartial to all.

s: Hui Tzŭ has many ideas
q: Hui Tzŭ was a man of many ideas.

s: universe is loved equally all creation (by Hui Tzŭ)
q: That he loves all creation equally

s: Kung Sun Lung is a dialectician (of the sophist class)
q: Huan T'uan and Kung Sun Lung were of this class.

s: dialecticians argue about Hui Tzŭ (without ever getting to the end)
q: And such was the stuff which dialecticians used to argue about with Hui Tzŭ, also without ever getting to the end of it.

s: dialecticians use specious premisses (to impose on people's minds)
q: By specious premisses they imposed on people's minds and drove them into false conclusions.

s: dialecticians drive into false conclusions (by specious premisses)
q: By specious premisses they imposed on people's minds and drove them into false conclusions.

s: THE UNIVERSE has no peer for Hui Tzŭ (according to Hui Tzŭ)
q: The universe does not hold my peer.

s: Hui Tzŭ has works filling five carts
q: His works would fill five carts.

s: Huang Liao asks about Earth (why it did not sink)
q: named Huang Liao, asked why the sky did not fall and the earth sink

s: Huang Liao asks about wind (its origin)
q: also, whence came wind, rain, and thunder.

s: TAO is a way of the universe
q: Looked at from the point of view of the TAO of the universe

s: TAO is exponent of Hui Tzŭ (dangerous for Hui Tzŭ to present himself as such)
q: But to let him put himself forward as an exponent of TAO, would have been dangerous indeed.

s: mosquito is compared with Hui Tzŭ (in value from the point of view of TAO)
q: the value of Hui Tzŭ may be compared with the efforts of a mosquito or a gadfly.

s: gadfly is compared with Hui Tzŭ (in value from the point of view of TAO)
q: the value of Hui Tzŭ may be compared with the efforts of a mosquito or a gadfly.

s: Chuang Tzŭ may be author of concluding chapter (according to Wang An Shih and Su Tung P'o)
q: Wang An Shih and Su Tung P'o both thought that it might well have come from the hand of Chuang Tzŭ.

s: Hui Tzŭ has doctrines Hui Tzŭ's doctrines
q: But his doctrines are paradoxical, and his terms are used ambiguously.

s: Hui Tzŭ is regarded as great philosopher
q: Accordingly, Hui Tzŭ was regarded as a great philosopher and a very subtle dialectician; and became a favourite with the other dialecticians of the day.

s: Hui Tzŭ is a favourite of dialecticians (of the day)
q: Accordingly, Hui Tzŭ was regarded as a great philosopher and a very subtle dialectician; and became a favourite with the other dialecticians of the day.

s: Hui Tzŭ devotes intelligence to dialecticians (daily, by advancing preposterous theses)
